note: All 24 why lines read against their study. Re-read today: Selcuk 2012 (Cornell write-up), Fingerman 2015/16 (full paper), Dreisoerner 2021 (write-up). The rest were checked in the Family review (19 Nov).

cards.note: The why line has no study in it, just the takeaway (rule D1). Add Liu 2023: "People underestimated how much reaching out meant, even to people they were close to."

Liu 2023 is about reaching out to friends and acquaintances, not family (rule D3). Fingerman's daily family study (#48) shows parents' moods lift on days with pleasant contact, which fits a family chat card.
Kumar and Epley 2018 letters went to anyone who'd helped them, mostly not family (rule D3). Worth looking for a study of thanking a family member.

Right (148 studies, about 50% better survival), but survival odds are a strange reason for a 20-year-old, and it isn't about chosen family. A study of chosen family or close ties and wellbeing would land better.

Mostly right: 159 adults, average age 21, self-soothing touch before a stress test lowered the stress hormone. The "18 to 35" range isn't confirmed in the write-up; say "young adults" unless the paper confirms it.
Right: in one experiment people looked at a photo of their mum after an upsetting memory and recovered faster. Another used a partner's photo.
Right: 247 parents aged 45 to 65, 7 days of calls; pleasant contact with grown children went with better daily moods. Published Dec 2015 (issue 2016).
Study is of 14 to 16 year olds (flagged and kept in the Family review). Still worth a study of young adults if one turns up.
Balban 2023: every group (breathing and mindfulness) got less anxious; what set long breaths out apart was a better mood. Say "left people in a better mood", as Rest #166 does.
